explanation: Fires on word-internal or function-word tokens in non-English text (Russian, Turkish, Japanese, Portuguese, Spanish, Swedish, Dutch, Romanian, etc.), especially mid-word suffix pieces and short particles like 'se', 'a', 'he'; the language of the context matters more than the specific token. English text gives at most weak activation.

Fires on a heterogeneous set of tokens: '<option value' in HTML select markup, digits inside numeric identifiers/OIDs, 'normal'/'N' in normal-distribution contexts, and assorted tokens in boilerplate phrases ('please feel free', 'please alert', 'or visit', '501(c)(3)'). No single shared feature.

Fires in source code on tokens that denote or open arrays/lists: array type names ('array', 'Array', 'vector', 'Vector'), '[' / '[]' brackets in declarations or literals, list quotes in Lisp, and closing parentheses of calls like Array.isArray(x) or split('&'). Prose gives little activation.

Fires in code on identifiers for results, responses, status, messages, and errors (e.g. lblMessage, getStatus, hResult, 'message', response.status, err, StandardError, success), especially in error handling or HTTP/AJAX response code. Weak elsewhere.

Fires on the second or later token of a multi-token technical or domain term, completing a compound noun phrase (hantavirus, fill factor, quantum efficiency, dividend yield, below knee, cord blood, Deepwater Horizon, Labor & Delivery), mostly in scientific/medical text. The preceding tokens set up the term; the marked token finishes it.

Fires on mid-word subword pieces of long scientific/chemical/biomedical words (cryptoxanthin, docosahexaenoic, follicular, polysaccharide, polymorphism, cyclohex-), especially prefixes like poly-/cyc-/follic-. Also some scattered non-English and boilerplate hits.

Fires on a digit token inside a multi-digit number, especially the middle zeros of large round numbers written with commas (157,000, 900,000, 650,000) like populations and counts. Other digit sequences fire moderately; non-numeric tokens barely fire.

Mixture: 'file'/'copy'/'for' in software license headers ('LICENSE file', 'received a copy'), 'want'/'wish to' in 'did not want to be named' anonymous-source phrases, and various noun tokens in scientific or news text. No clear single concept.

Fires on tokens about mixtures and solutions in chemistry/materials text: the '/v' in concentration units like v/v or w/v, and words for colloids, dispersions, emulsions, suspensions, solutes and dispersants. Composition phrases like 'by weight' or 'basis' fire moderately.

Fires on the comma right after a sentence-opening adverbial or introductory phrase (However, Therefore, In this case, In 1998, Here, Eventually). Other clause-boundary connectives (where, but, that) fire moderately; commas inside lists or mid-clause fire little.
No clear pattern: hits include 'another', thousands-separator commas in numbers, 'this' in license headers, 'made up', unit prefixes, and assorted code tokens. Looks like a mixture.

Mostly fires on tokens in inorganic-chemistry and materials text naming chemical compounds, elements, acids/bases and their links ('(' before a chemical formula, 'with calcium', lithium, aluminum, hydrolysis). Separately fires on the first digit of the year after 'Copyright (c)' in code headers.

Fires on the first subword piece of a proper name or rare word split into several tokens, especially surname starts after a first name (Sch-, Ro-, Hos-, Hus-, Gh-), and 'Ind' in 'Individually' in legal captions. Driven by the word being an unfamiliar multi-token name.

Fires on subword pieces inside technical words, acronyms or code terms (keyframes, iFrame, germ-free, cytokeratin, the F in IRF4/GCTF/CRF), with no clear shared meaning; a scattered mixture of word fragments.
